title: Counterfactual timeout-policy simulations for continuous scheduling
content:
Purpose and motivation:
We need to understand how alternative timeout/flush policies would have behaved under real production traffic without risking live changes. Rather than incremental online experiments (which are slow and risky for customers), we built a counterfactual simulation harness that replays traces and computes latency, fairness, and throughput outcomes for a set of timeout variants. This doc records the simulation design, initial hypotheses, key findings, and recommended next actions.

High-level goals:
- Quantify p50/p95/p99 effect of different timeout policies (fixed, dynamic slack, deadline-slack, and urgency-weighted).
- Measure fairness regressions across tenant classes (free/dev, paid, enterprise) under each policy.
- Evaluate throughput and GPU utilization impact vs latency gains.
- Surface scenarios where counterfactual simulation disagrees with small-scale live probes.

Why counterfactuals?
- Can run many variants quickly against the same workload traces and profile tails deterministically.
- Eliminates rollout noise (autoscaling artifacts, transient infra events) so policy signal is clearer.
- Enables per-request attribution of what would have changed (which requests had earlier flush, which were deferred).

Data & traces used:
- Production microtrace replay from 2025-09-14 to 2025-09-21 (high-traffic week, includes a 1-hour microburst on 2025-09-18). Trace anonymized (tenant ids hashed).
- Synthetic inter-arrival traces: heavy-tailed arrival generator to stress tails (Pareto alpha=1.4), paired with short/long prompt mixes.
- Small probe traces from canary environment (2025-10-09) used to cross-check simulator fidelity.

Hardware / model context used in simulation:
- Model family: redwood-3B-quant4 (serving config matched to prod kernel latencies).
- GPU profile: A100 40GB equivalence (we use measured per-token kernel latency curves from infra bench repo).
- Batch kernel shape approximations: short prompt and long prompt latencies captured separately.

Simulator design notes:
- Input: sequence of request arrival events with metadata (tenant class, desired response length, prefill token count, priority).
- Queue model: per-core queue with continuous-batcher semantics (requests coalesce until flush condition).
- Timeout policy abstraction: a small DSL that supports fixed-timeout, deadline-slack (deadline = request.deadline or service SLO; slack adjusts based on queue age), urgency-weighted (priority increases effective age), and dynamic-adaptive (timeout computed from recent quantile feedback).
- KV-cache and prefill logic: simulated token-wise prefill to preserve prefill-driven flushes.
- Resource model: simple GPU occupancy accounting with service time approximated from measured kernels; no explicit network variability.
- Output: per-request simulated start_time, flush_time, finish_time, batch_size_on_flush, and simulated token-cost.

Validation checks (sanity & fidelity):
- Replayed the canary probe traces and compared simulated p95/p99 to observed within ±7% for stable periods. Discrepancies noted during autoscaler churn windows — excluded from core analysis.
- Cross-checked average batch size distribution vs production histograms; simulator captures median and 90th percentile within reasonable tolerance.

Policies evaluated (variants):
1) baseline-fixed-20ms: fixed flush timeout 20ms (current canary baseline).
2) fixed-10ms: aggressive fixed timeout.
3) deadline-slack-quantile: set per-request timeout = min(default, slack computed from per-tenant 95th of queueing delay * 0.6).
4) urgency-gain: effective age = real age + urgency_weight * tenant_priority (urgency_weight tuned to 15ms per priority step).
5) adaptive-anneal: timeout starts high (40ms) and anneals to 12ms as recent p99 improves.
6) hybrid-prefill-trigger: prefill token count threshold forces immediate flush if prefill > X (X tuned in sweep).

Key metrics captured:
- Latency percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99/p999) measured end-to-end simulated finish_time - arrival_time.
- Batch size on flush distribution and mean GPU tokens per batch.
- Fairness delta: change in p99 for tenant class relative to baseline.
- Throughput (requests/s) and simulated GPU utilization proxy (tokens-in-flight / max-capacity).
- Abort/retry count (cases where simulated policy forces shed or fallback).

Initial hypotheses (pre-sim):
- Reducing fixed timeouts will reduce median latency but blow up p99 due to smaller batches and kernel inefficiency.
- Deadline-slack and urgency-guided approaches will keep p99 under control while still reducing median.
- Adaptive policies may oscillate under bursty load unless annealed carefully.

Findings (summary):
- fixed-10ms: median improved by ~18% vs baseline, but p99 regressed by +42% in the production trace due to many prefill-heavy long requests that lost batching efficiency.
- deadline-slack-quantile: median improved ~12%, p99 improved slightly (-6%) for paid tenants and stayed neutral for enterprise; free/dev tenants saw a small p99 regression (+8%) because the slack heuristic favored higher-paying tenants.
- urgency-gain: showed the best fairness profile — enterprise p99 improved (-9%), paid neutral, free/dev p99 increased (+4%) but within acceptable SLO guardrail. Overall GPU utilization decreased 6%, token cost per response up slightly.
- adaptive-anneal: delivered stable p95 improvements but occasional oscillation during the 1-hour microburst gave transient p99 spikes; adding a minimum hold window (30s) suppressed oscillations in follow-up sim.
- hybrid-prefill-trigger: extremely effective at preserving p99 for long-prefill requests while allowing short ones to flush faster — gave a balanced median (-14%) and p99 (-2%).

Per-tenant fairness breakdown (notable):
- Free/dev tenants experienced proportionally more p99 regressions when policies prioritized urgency by monetary tier. This points to a potential SLA-visible effect; must avoid regressions beyond a small tolerance for free tier to avoid developer churn.

Case study: microburst at 2025-09-18 14:03
- Under fixed-10ms, many long requests were flushed early as small single-request batches, triggering kernel inefficiency and cascading tail latency.
- Deadline-slack and hybrid-prefill held long requests in queue longer and benefited from queued coalescence during the burst, preventing the p99 spike. Adaptive-anneal without hold window reacted too quickly and briefly worsened p99.

Observability artifacts and where to look in prod if we probe: 
- tracer spans to compare simulated vs observed start/finish times: span names 'batch.wait' and 'batch.flush' were most informative.
- Per-tenant p99 trendline by hour and batch-size histogram by minute.

Design implications and recommended immediate actions:
1) Do a two-week canary of hybrid-prefill-trigger + urgency-gain combined but with conservative urgency_weight (half current simulation value). Canary: route 2% of traffic in non-critical region. Linked ticket: INF-842.
2) Implement minimum hold window (30s) in adaptive-anneal controller to avoid oscillation during bursts; run sim sweep to tune hold length and learning rate.
3) Add per-tenant fairness guardrail: cap allowed p99 regression for free/dev to +10% relative to baseline; if triggered, auto-fallback to baseline policy for that tenant.
4) Expand simulator fidelity: add a simple autoscaler noise model and occasional infra noise spikes (we saw sim vs prod mismatch around autoscaling events).

Open questions / next experiments:
- How does hybrid-prefill interact with quantized kernel shapes at long sequence lengths (we relied on approximations)? Need kernel-level validation.
- Is a monetary-tier-based urgency schema acceptable product-wise? Product input required (impact on developer experience).
- Can we build a fast in-cluster real-time counterfactual probe that computes per-request "would have waited" tags live for a % of requests?

Action items (owners & ETA):
- Priya: open canary run plan and coordinate infra for 2% traffic split (ETA: 2025-11-30).
- Marcus: implement minimum hold window in control loop (PR draft: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4132) (ETA: 1 week).
- Alex: extend simulator to include simple autoscaler churn model and run extended week-long traces (ETA: 2 weeks).
- Sofia: sync with product on tier-based urgency policy acceptability and prepare customer-facing notes (ETA: 1 week).

Appendix: quick reproducibility notes
- Repo: serving-runtime/sim/harness (branch: simulations/counterfactual-timeout-2025).
- Command to run representative sweep: ./run_sim_sweep --trace traces/2025-09-week1.avro --policy-set config/policies/timeout_sweep.yaml --out results/cf_timeout_20251103.tar.gz
- Key scripts: tools/compute_fairness_delta.py, analysis/plot_batch_hist.py

Notes and loose thoughts (scratch):
- Consider exposing a per-tenant "latency budget" parameter to the scheduler API so customers can trade cost vs tail themselves.
- We should add a lightweight per-request annotation in traces when a flush is forced by prefill threshold; that will make later attribution easier.

If you review this, please comment inline on the policy DSL semantics or on the proposed guardrail thresholds. For testing, look first at the microburst window example — the different policies diverge very visibly there and it's the fastest way to validate simulator changes.

End of doc.
